question.scenario: A 56-year-old man presents with sharp anterior chest pain 4 days after inferior STEMI treated with successful PCI. The pain is worse with deep inspiration and lying flat, and better when sitting forward. He has a low-grade fever of 37.8°C. Examination reveals a pericardial friction rub. ECG shows diffuse ST-segment elevation (different from his original ECG which showed ST-elevation only in leads II, III, aVF). Troponin I is mildly elevated at 0.6 ng/mL (down from 8.2 ng/mL on admission). Echocardiography shows a small pericardial effusion (6 mm) with no tamponade.
question.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis, and what is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Recurrent myocardial infarction; urgent repeat angiography and PCI
options.B: Acute pericarditis (post-MI pericarditis); NSAIDs and colchicine
options.D: Pulmonary embolism; commence anticoagulation with heparin

mcqs.explanation: Post-myocardial infarction pericarditis (also called early pericarditis or acute pericarditis complicating MI) occurs in 5-20% of STEMI patients in the modern era (historically higher before early reperfusion). It typically develops 2-7 days post-MI and is caused by inflammatory reaction to transmural myocardial necrosis, where necrotic myocardium adjacent to the pericardium triggers pericardial inflammation. This differs from Dressler syndrome (late post-MI pericarditis), which occurs weeks to months post-MI and has an autoimmune mechanism. Clinical features of post-MI pericarditis: (1) Timing: 2-7 days post-MI (median 3-4 days); (2) Chest pain: Sharp, pleuritic, positional (worse lying flat, better sitting forward), worse with deep inspiration; distinct from ischaemic chest pain; (3) Pericardial friction rub: Scratchy, high-pitched sound best heard at left sternal border with patient leaning forward, may be transient (present in 30-50% of cases); (4) Low-grade fever: 37.5-38.5°C; (5) ECG: Diffuse ST-elevation (concave upward, different distribution from original MI), PR-segment depression (classical pericarditis finding); (6) Troponin: May be mildly elevated or declining from initial MI peak; (7) Pericardial effusion: Small to moderate effusion common (50-70% of cases), large effusions and tamponade rare (<5%). Differential diagnosis for post-MI chest pain: Using a systematic approach to differentiate various causes of chest pain 4 days post-MI: (1) Post-MI pericarditis (Option B): CORRECT DIAGNOSIS. This patient has classic features: (a) Timing: 4 days post-MI (typical for early pericarditis); (b) Pleuritic, positional chest pain distinct from original ischaemic pain; (c) Pericardial friction rub (pathognomonic); (d) Low-grade fever; (e) Diffuse ST-elevation on ECG (different distribution from original inferior MI which had ST-elevation only in leads II, III, aVF); (f) Troponin declining from initial MI peak but mildly elevated (consistent with resolving MI, not recurrent MI); (g) Small pericardial effusion without tamponade. These features conclusively indicate post-MI pericarditis. (2) Recurrent myocardial infarction (Option A): UNLIKELY. While recurrent MI is a concern in post-MI patients, the clinical features argue against it: (a) Chest pain character: Sharp, pleuritic, positional pain is NOT typical of ischaemic pain (which is dull, pressure-like, exertional); (b) Pericardial friction rub: NOT a feature of MI; (c) Diffuse ST-elevation: Recurrent MI would show ST-elevation in a specific coronary territory (e.g., anterior if LAD occlusion, inferior if RCA occlusion), not diffuse; (d) Troponin trend: Declining from initial peak (0.6 ng/mL vs. 8.2 ng/mL on admission) suggests resolving initial MI, not new MI. Recurrent MI would show rising troponin trend. Clinical context (pleuritic pain, friction rub, diffuse ST-elevation) strongly favours pericarditis, not recurrent MI. Urgent angiography is NOT indicated. (3) Cardiac tamponade (Option C): INCORRECT. While this patient has a pericardial effusion, it is SMALL (6 mm) and echo shows NO tamponade. Cardiac tamponade is a clinical diagnosis with haemodynamic compromise: (a) Beck's triad: Hypotension, elevated JVP, muffled heart sounds; (b) Pulsus paradoxus: Drop in systolic BP >10 mmHg on inspiration; (c) Echocardiographic signs: Right atrial/ventricular diastolic collapse, respiratory variation in mitral/tricuspid inflow velocities; (d) Haemodynamic instability: Tachycardia, hypotension, oliguria. This patient has none of these features. Small pericardial effusions post-MI are common and benign, requiring observation but not pericardiocentesis. Urgent pericardiocentesis is indicated only for tamponade (haemodynamic compromise) or very large effusions (>20 mm). (4) Pulmonary embolism (Option D): UNLIKELY. While PE is a differential for post-MI chest pain (immobility, hypercoagulable state), the clinical features favour pericarditis: (a) Pleuritic chest pain is common in both PE and pericarditis, but positional component (better sitting forward) and pericardial friction rub are specific to pericarditis; (b) PE typically presents with dyspnoea, tachycardia, hypoxaemia, and sometimes haemoptysis; (c) ECG in PE shows sinus tachycardia, S1Q3T3 pattern, or right heart strain (not diffuse ST-elevation); (d) No mention of dyspnoea, hypoxaemia, or risk factors for PE (prolonged immobility, DVT symptoms). If PE suspected, D-dimer, CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA), and/or V/Q scan would be indicated, but pericarditis is the correct diagnosis here. Management of post-MI pericarditis: (1) First-line therapy: ASPIRIN at high dose (650-1000 mg every 6-8 hours) for 1-2 weeks, then taper. Aspirin is preferred over NSAIDs post-MI because NSAIDs may interfere with myocardial healing and increase risk of adverse remodelling, myocardial rupture, and recurrent MI. However, aspirin has lower risk of these complications. (2) COLCHICINE: 0.5-0.6 mg twice daily for 3 months. Colchicine reduces pericarditis duration, symptom severity, and recurrence risk (COPPS trial, CORP trial). It is safe post-MI and recommended as adjunct to aspirin. Option B lists NSAIDs + colchicine, but technically aspirin (high-dose) + colchicine is more accurate post-MI. However, Option B is the closest correct answer, as the principle is anti-inflammatory therapy + colchicine. (3) AVOID or use NSAIDs cautiously: Ibuprofen, indomethacin, and other NSAIDs are generally AVOIDED in post-MI pericarditis (especially in first 1-2 weeks post-MI) due to potential for impaired infarct healing, increased infarct expansion, ventricular rupture risk, and adverse cardiovascular outcomes. If aspirin fails or is contraindicated, low-dose ibuprofen or indomethacin may be used cautiously, but aspirin preferred. (4) Corticosteroids: AVOID unless refractory pericarditis unresponsive to aspirin/colchicine, as steroids increase recurrence risk and may impair infarct healing. Reserve for severe cases or contraindications to aspirin/colchicine. (5) Symptomatic relief: Sitting forward posture, avoid lying flat. (6) Monitor for complications: Cardiac tamponade (rare), recurrent pericarditis (10-20% risk), constrictive pericarditis (very rare). Serial echocardiography if effusion enlarges or symptoms worsen. (7) Continue standard post-MI therapy: Dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor), beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor, statin. Do not stop antiplatelet therapy due to pericarditis risk; bleeding risk from pericarditis is low. Dressler syndrome (late post-MI pericarditis): Occurs weeks to months post-MI (median 2-3 weeks, range 1 week to several months), caused by autoimmune reaction to myocardial antigens exposed during MI. Clinical features similar to early pericarditis (pleuritic chest pain, fever, pericardial friction rub, pericardial effusion) but also includes pleural effusions, elevated inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP), and sometimes pulmonary infiltrates. Treatment is similar (aspirin, colchicine, occasionally corticosteroids if severe). Dressler syndrome is now rare (<1% of MIs) due to early reperfusion therapy limiting infarct size. Prognosis: Post-MI pericarditis is generally benign with good prognosis. Symptoms typically resolve within 1-2 weeks with treatment. Recurrence occurs in 10-20% of cases. Cardiac tamponade is rare (<5%). Constrictive pericarditis is extremely rare (<1%). Post-MI pericarditis does not significantly increase mortality or long-term morbidity if managed appropriately. Safety-netting: Educate patient about warning signs of cardiac tamponade (worsening dyspnoea, lightheadedness, syncope, chest pressure) and recurrent pericarditis (recurrent pleuritic chest pain). If symptoms worsen or fail to improve with treatment, repeat echocardiography to assess effusion size. Differentiate pericarditis pain from recurrent ischaemic pain (if typical ischaemic pain develops, seek urgent medical attention). Follow-up with cardiologist at 2-4 weeks. In summary, this patient has post-MI pericarditis (early pericarditis complicating inferior STEMI), presenting 4 days post-MI with pleuritic positional chest pain, pericardial friction rub, low-grade fever, diffuse ST-elevation, and small pericardial effusion. Management is high-dose aspirin (preferred post-MI) plus colchicine for 3 months. Avoid NSAIDs if possible due to potential impairment of infarct healing. Prognosis is good with appropriate treatment.

mcqs.summary: Post-MI pericarditis occurs in 5-20% of STEMI patients, typically 2-7 days post-MI, caused by inflammatory reaction to transmural necrosis. Clinical features: pleuritic positional chest pain, pericardial friction rub, low-grade fever, diffuse ST-elevation, small pericardial effusion. Differs from recurrent MI (regional ST-elevation, rising troponin, no friction rub) and Dressler syndrome (weeks-months post-MI, autoimmune). Management: High-dose aspirin (preferred post-MI) + colchicine for 3 months. Avoid NSAIDs (impair infarct healing). Prognosis generally benign.

question.scenario: A 62-year-old woman presents with fever (38.5°C), pleuritic chest pain, and dyspnoea 3 weeks after anterior STEMI treated with primary PCI. She also complains of malaise and arthralgia. On examination, she has a pericardial friction rub and bilateral pleural effusions on chest X-ray. Blood tests show elevated ESR 85 mm/hr (normal <20) and CRP 120 mg/L (normal <5). Echocardiography shows a moderate pericardial effusion (12 mm) with no tamponade. She had been recovering well until 2 days ago when symptoms began.
question.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis, and how does it differ from post-MI pericarditis?

options.A: Post-MI pericarditis (early pericarditis); occurs 2-7 days post-MI due to transmural necrosis
options.B: Dressler syndrome (post-myocardial infarction syndrome); occurs weeks-months post-MI with autoimmune mechanism, includes pleural effusions and systemic features
options.C: Infective endocarditis; requires blood cultures and prolonged antibiotic therapy
options.D: Pulmonary embolism with pleural effusions; requires anticoagulation

mcqs.explanation: Dressler syndrome (also called post-myocardial infarction syndrome or post-cardiac injury syndrome) is a late form of pericarditis occurring weeks to months after myocardial infarction, cardiac surgery, or other cardiac injury. It is distinct from early post-MI pericarditis, which occurs in the first week post-MI. Dressler syndrome is now rare (<1% of MIs) in the modern era due to early reperfusion therapy limiting infarct size, but remains an important differential diagnosis for post-MI complications. Pathophysiology: Dressler syndrome is believed to be an AUTOIMMUNE phenomenon triggered by exposure of cardiac antigens (from myocardial necrosis) to the immune system, leading to antibody formation against cardiac tissue. The immune response targets the pericardium, pleura, and occasionally lung parenchyma, causing inflammation. This differs from early post-MI pericarditis, which is a direct inflammatory reaction to adjacent transmural myocardial necrosis without autoimmune component. Clinical features of Dressler syndrome: (1) Timing: Typically 2-12 weeks post-MI (median 3-4 weeks), though can occur 1 week to several months post-MI. Contrast with early post-MI pericarditis which occurs 2-7 days post-MI. (2) Chest pain: Pleuritic, positional (worse lying flat, better sitting forward), sharp. May also have pericardial or pleuritic pain (from pleural effusions). (3) Fever: Often higher than early pericarditis (38-39°C), with malaise and systemic symptoms. (4) Pericardial involvement: Pericardial friction rub, pericardial effusion (small to large, occasionally causing tamponade). (5) PLEURAL INVOLVEMENT: Pleural effusions (unilateral or bilateral) in 50-70% of cases. This is a KEY distinguishing feature from early post-MI pericarditis, which rarely causes pleural effusions. (6) Pulmonary infiltrates: Occasionally present, likely from immune-mediated pneumonitis. (7) Systemic features: Arthralgia, myalgia, malaise, anorexia. More prominent than in early pericarditis. (8) Elevated inflammatory markers: ESR and CRP markedly elevated (often ESR >50 mm/hr, CRP >50 mg/L), more pronounced than early pericarditis. (9) Leukocytosis: Elevated WBC count. (10) Recurrence: 20-30% recurrence rate, higher than early pericarditis (10-20%). Differential diagnosis: Using a systematic approach to differentiate Dressler syndrome from other post-MI complications: (1) Dressler syndrome (Option B): CORRECT DIAGNOSIS. This patient has classic features: (a) Timing: 3 weeks post-MI (typical for Dressler syndrome, not early pericarditis which occurs 2-7 days post-MI); (b) Fever, pleuritic chest pain, pericardial friction rub, pericardial effusion; (c) PLEURAL EFFUSIONS (bilateral): Hallmark of Dressler syndrome, distinguishing it from early post-MI pericarditis; (d) Systemic symptoms: Malaise, arthralgia; (e) Markedly elevated inflammatory markers: ESR 85 mm/hr, CRP 120 mg/L; (f) Clinical course: Recovering well post-MI, then sudden onset of symptoms at 3 weeks. These features conclusively indicate Dressler syndrome (post-myocardial infarction syndrome). (2) Post-MI pericarditis/early pericarditis (Option A): INCORRECT. While this patient has pericarditis, the TIMING (3 weeks post-MI) and presence of PLEURAL EFFUSIONS distinguish Dressler syndrome from early post-MI pericarditis. Early post-MI pericarditis occurs 2-7 days post-MI, is caused by direct inflammation from transmural necrosis, and does NOT typically cause pleural effusions or marked systemic symptoms. The clinical picture here is classic for Dressler syndrome, not early pericarditis. KEY DIFFERENCES: (a) Timing: Early pericarditis 2-7 days post-MI; Dressler syndrome 2-12 weeks post-MI; (b) Mechanism: Early pericarditis = direct inflammation from necrosis; Dressler = autoimmune; (c) Pleural effusions: Rare in early pericarditis; common in Dressler syndrome (50-70%); (d) Systemic symptoms: Mild in early pericarditis; prominent in Dressler syndrome; (e) Inflammatory markers: Mildly elevated in early pericarditis; markedly elevated in Dressler syndrome. (3) Infective endocarditis (Option C): UNLIKELY. While endocarditis causes fever, it typically presents with continuous bacteraemia (positive blood cultures), new or changing heart murmur, embolic phenomena (splinter haemorrhages, Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, Roth spots), and vegetations on echocardiography (usually seen on valves, not pericardium). This patient's presentation (pleuritic chest pain, pericardial friction rub, pleural effusions, pericardial effusion without valve vegetations) is NOT consistent with endocarditis. Endocarditis is also uncommon 3 weeks post-PCI without indwelling lines or recent bacteraemia. If endocarditis suspected, blood cultures (3 sets from different sites) and transoesophageal echocardiography (TEE) would be indicated, but Dressler syndrome is the correct diagnosis here. (4) Pulmonary embolism (Option D): UNLIKELY. While PE can cause pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea, and pleural effusions, it does NOT explain: (a) Pericardial friction rub and pericardial effusion (NOT features of PE); (b) Fever and markedly elevated inflammatory markers (PE may cause mild fever and elevated D-dimer, but not ESR 85 mm/hr and CRP 120 mg/L); (c) Systemic symptoms (arthralgia, malaise). PE typically presents with sudden dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain, hypoxaemia, tachycardia, and sometimes haemoptysis. ECG may show S1Q3T3 or right heart strain. D-dimer is elevated. Diagnosis confirmed by CTPA or V/Q scan. If PE suspected, anticoagulation would be indicated, but the clinical picture strongly favours Dressler syndrome, not PE. Management of Dressler syndrome: (1) First-line therapy: ASPIRIN at high dose (650-1000 mg every 6-8 hours) for 1-2 weeks, then taper over 2-4 weeks. Aspirin is preferred over NSAIDs post-MI due to lower risk of adverse myocardial remodelling. (2) COLCHICINE: 0.5-0.6 mg twice daily for 3 months. Colchicine significantly reduces symptom duration, recurrence risk, and need for hospitalisation (COPE trial, ICAP trial). Colchicine is safe and well-tolerated (main side effect: diarrhoea 10-20%). (3) NSAIDs: Ibuprofen 600-800 mg three times daily or indomethacin 25-50 mg three times daily may be used if aspirin fails, but generally avoided within first 4 weeks post-MI due to potential impairment of infarct healing. After 4 weeks post-MI (as in this case), NSAIDs are safer but aspirin still preferred. (4) CORTICOSTEROIDS: Reserved for severe or refractory cases unresponsive to aspirin/NSAIDs and colchicine. Prednisone 0.25-0.5 mg/kg/day for 1-2 weeks, then slow taper. Corticosteroids increase recurrence risk and should be avoided as first-line therapy. Use only if severe symptoms, large pericardial effusion approaching tamponade, or failure of aspirin/colchicine. (5) Monitor for complications: Cardiac tamponade (rare but possible, especially with large effusions); recurrence (20-30% risk, treated with repeat course of aspirin/colchicine); constrictive pericarditis (very rare, <1%). (6) Pleural effusions: Small pleural effusions are common and benign, requiring no specific treatment. Large effusions causing dyspnoea may require therapeutic thoracentesis. (7) Continue standard post-MI therapy: Dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin for pericarditis + P2Y12 inhibitor), beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor, statin. Do not stop antiplatelet therapy; bleeding risk is low. (8) Activity restriction: Avoid strenuous physical activity until symptoms resolve and inflammatory markers normalise. Prognosis: Dressler syndrome is generally benign with good prognosis if treated appropriately. Symptoms typically resolve within 2-4 weeks with treatment. Recurrence is common (20-30%), usually within 3-6 months, and treated with repeat course of aspirin/colchicine. Cardiac tamponade occurs in <5% of cases. Constrictive pericarditis is very rare (<1%). Dressler syndrome does not significantly increase long-term mortality if managed appropriately. Historical context: Dressler syndrome was described by Dr. William Dressler in 1956 and was common in the pre-reperfusion era (incidence 3-5% of MIs). With the advent of primary PCI and thrombolysis, which limit infarct size, Dressler syndrome has become rare (<1% of MIs in modern era). However, it still occurs occasionally and remains an important differential for post-MI chest pain presenting weeks to months after MI. Safety-netting: Educate patient about recurrence risk (20-30%) and warning signs (recurrent pleuritic chest pain, fever, dyspnoea). If symptoms recur, repeat course of aspirin/colchicine. Monitor for signs of cardiac tamponade (worsening dyspnoea, lightheadedness, syncope). Follow-up with cardiologist at 2-4 weeks and repeat echocardiography if effusion large or symptoms worsen. In summary, this patient has Dressler syndrome (post-myocardial infarction syndrome), presenting 3 weeks post-MI with fever, pleuritic chest pain, pericardial and pleural effusions, systemic symptoms, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers. Key differences from early post-MI pericarditis: timing (weeks vs. days), pleural involvement (common vs. rare), mechanism (autoimmune vs. direct inflammation). Management: high-dose aspirin + colchicine for 3 months, reserve corticosteroids for refractory cases. Prognosis is good, though recurrence common (20-30%).

Differs from early post-MI pericarditis (2-7 days, direct inflammation): (1) Timing (weeks vs. days); (2) Pleural effusions common in Dressler (50-70%), rare in early pericarditis; (3) Systemic symptoms prominent in Dressler (fever, malaise, arthralgia); (4) Markedly elevated inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP). question.scenario: A 68-year-old man is recovering from anterior STEMI treated with primary PCI 6 weeks ago. He has developed progressive dyspnoea on exertion and occasional palpitations. Echocardiography shows LVEF 35% with a large apical dyskinetic segment that bulges outward during systole (dyskinesia). Colour Doppler shows turbulent flow within the apical region. No thrombus is visualized.
question.stem: What complication has developed, and what are the main concerns?

options.A: Ventricular septal defect requiring urgent surgical repair
options.B: Left ventricular aneurysm; main risks are heart failure, arrhythmias, and thromboembolism
options.C: Free wall rupture; requires immediate pericardiocentesis and surgery
options.D: Acute mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle rupture; requires urgent surgery

mcqs.explanation: Left ventricular aneurysm is a late complication of transmural myocardial infarction, defined as a discrete area of dyskinetic myocardial wall that bulges outward (paradoxical motion) during systole. True LV aneurysms have a wide neck and involve all three layers of the ventricular wall (endocardium, myocardium, epicardium). They develop in 5-10% of MIs (more common with anterior/apical MIs and delayed/absent reperfusion). The pathophysiology involves transmural infarction leading to myocardial scar formation, which weakens and stretches over time, eventually forming a thin-walled outpouching that does not contract (akinesia) or paradoxically expands during systole (dyskinesia). Diagnostic features of LV aneurysm: (1) Timing: Develops weeks to months post-MI (median 6-8 weeks), as this case illustrates (6 weeks post-MI); (2) Echocardiographic findings: (a) Dyskinesia: Paradoxical outward bulging during systole (key feature distinguishing aneurysm from akinesia); (b) Wide neck: Aneurysm communicates with LV cavity via broad opening; (c) Thin wall: Aneurysmal wall is thin and scarred; (d) Turbulent flow: Swirling blood flow within aneurysm (seen on colour Doppler) predisposes to thrombus formation; (e) Location: Most common at apex (anterior/apical MIs from LAD occlusion); (3) Cardiac MRI: Gold standard for diagnosis and characterization. Shows late gadolinium enhancement (scar), wall thinning, and dyskinesia; (4) Ventriculography: Classic appearance of discrete outpouching during systole; (5) Chest X-ray: May show abnormal cardiac silhouette (apical bulge) or calcification (chronic aneurysms can calcify); (6) ECG: Persistent ST-segment elevation weeks to months post-MI (unlike normal evolution where ST-elevation resolves). Persistent ST-elevation suggests transmural scar with aneurysm. Differential diagnosis of post-MI complications: This patient has progressive heart failure symptoms (dyspnoea on exertion) and palpitations (arrhythmias) 6 weeks post-anterior MI, with echo showing apical dyskinesia and turbulent flow. Let's differentiate LV aneurysm from other mechanical complications: (1) Left ventricular aneurysm (Option B): CORRECT. This patient has classic features: (a) Timing: 6 weeks post-MI (typical for aneurysm development); (b) Anterior MI location (most common site for aneurysm); (c) Echocardiographic findings: Large apical dyskinetic segment bulging outward during systole (pathognomonic for aneurysm), turbulent flow within aneurysm; (d) Progressive heart failure symptoms (dyspnoea on exertion from reduced LV function); (e) Palpitations (arrhythmias from scar tissue providing substrate for re-entrant VT). Main concerns/complications of LV aneurysm: (1) HEART FAILURE: Aneurysm reduces effective stroke volume and cardiac output (blood pools in non-contractile aneurysmal segment rather than being ejected). Leads to progressive LV dysfunction, heart failure symptoms, and reduced exercise tolerance. (2) ARRHYTHMIAS: Aneurysmal scar provides substrate for ventricular tachycardia (VT) via re-entrant circuits. VT is common (30-50% of LV aneurysm patients develop VT) and can cause palpitations, syncope, or sudden cardiac death. (3) THROMBOEMBOLISM: Stagnant blood flow within aneurysm predisposes to LV thrombus formation (occurs in 30-50% of aneurysms). Thrombus can embolize, causing stroke (15-20% risk over 5 years), peripheral arterial embolism, or mesenteric ischaemia. (4) Aneurysm rupture: RARE with true aneurysms (unlike pseudoaneurysms which have high rupture risk). True aneurysms are contained by all three wall layers and pericardium, making rupture uncommon. (2) Ventricular septal defect (VSD) - Option A: INCORRECT. Post-MI VSD is an acute mechanical complication occurring 3-7 days post-MI (not 6 weeks), when infarcted septum is weakest. Clinical presentation: Sudden haemodynamic deterioration, new harsh pansystolic murmur at left sternal border with thrill, step-up in oxygen saturation from RA to RV (on right heart catheterisation), and septal defect visible on echo with left-to-right shunt. This patient has NO murmur mentioned, NO acute deterioration, and echo shows apical dyskinesia (not septal defect). VSD would require urgent surgical repair due to high mortality without intervention. This is NOT VSD. (3) Free wall rupture (Option C): INCORRECT. Free wall rupture is a catastrophic complication occurring acutely (typically 3-7 days post-MI, range 1-14 days) when infarcted myocardium is weakest. Clinical presentation: Sudden cardiovascular collapse, cardiac tamponade (Beck's triad: hypotension, elevated JVP, muffled heart sounds), pulseless electrical activity (PEA) cardiac arrest, or sudden death. Diagnosis: Echo shows pericardial effusion with tamponade physiology, often with visible defect in LV wall. Management: Emergency pericardiocentesis (temporizing) followed by immediate surgical repair, though mortality is >90% despite intervention. This patient is stable 6 weeks post-MI with no tamponade, so free wall rupture is NOT the diagnosis. (4) Acute mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle rupture (Option D): INCORRECT. Papillary muscle rupture is an acute mechanical complication (typically 3-7 days post-MI, especially with inferior MI affecting posteromedial papillary muscle). Clinical presentation: Sudden onset severe dyspnoea, pulmonary oedema, cardiogenic shock, new loud holosystolic murmur at apex radiating to axilla (though murmur may be soft if severe MR and equalization of LA/LV pressures). Echo shows flail mitral leaflet, severe MR, and ruptured papillary muscle head. Management: Emergency surgical mitral valve repair or replacement. This patient has NO murmur mentioned, NO acute deterioration, and echo shows apical dyskinesia (not MR or papillary muscle abnormality). This is NOT acute MR. Management of LV aneurysm: (1) Medical therapy (standard heart failure management): (a) ACE inhibitors or ARBs: Reduce afterload, prevent adverse remodelling, improve survival (e.g., ramipril, perindopril, enalapril, candesartan); (b) Beta-blockers: Reduce arrhythmia risk, improve LV function, improve survival (e.g., metoprolol, bisoprolol, carvedilol); (c) Diuretics: For symptom relief if fluid overload (furosemide, bumetanide); (d) Aldosterone antagonists: If LVEF <40% and heart failure symptoms (spironolactone, eplerenone); (e) Consider SGLT2 inhibitors: Empagliflozin, dapagliflozin (proven mortality benefit in heart failure with reduced EF). (2) Anticoagulation: If LV thrombus present on echo, anticoagulate with warfarin (target INR 2-3) or DOAC (rivaroxaban, apixaban) for at least 3-6 months, sometimes indefinitely. If no thrombus visualized (as in this case), anticoagulation is NOT routinely indicated for aneurysm alone, though some experts consider it if large aneurysm with significant flow stasis. Continue dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor) for 12 months post-MI per standard ACS guidelines. (3) ICD (implantable cardioverter-defibrillator): If LVEF <35% despite 3 months of optimal medical therapy, ICD is indicated for primary prevention of sudden cardiac death (Class I indication). This patient has LVEF 35% and likely meets ICD criteria if LV function does not improve. If sustained VT occurs, ICD is immediately indicated (secondary prevention). (4) Surgical aneurysmectomy: Reserved for: (a) Large aneurysm with severe heart failure symptoms refractory to medical therapy; (b) Recurrent VT despite medical therapy and ICD; (c) LV thrombus refractory to anticoagulation with recurrent embolic events; (d) Often combined with CABG if significant residual coronary disease. Surgical mortality is 5-10%. Surgery is NOT routinely indicated for asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic aneurysms well-controlled on medical therapy. This patient may benefit from aneurysmectomy if heart failure progresses despite optimal medical therapy. (5) Monitor for thrombus: Serial echocardiography every 3-6 months to assess for LV thrombus development. If thrombus develops, initiate anticoagulation. Prognosis: LV aneurysm increases mortality compared to post-MI patients without aneurysm, primarily due to heart failure, arrhythmias, and thromboembolism. Five-year survival is 70-80% with medical therapy. Prognosis improves with optimal heart failure management, ICD if indicated, and anticoagulation if thrombus present. Surgical aneurysmectomy may improve outcomes in selected patients with severe symptoms. Safety-netting: Educate patient about warning signs: worsening dyspnoea (heart failure decompensation), palpitations or syncope (VT), sudden neurological symptoms (embolic stroke from LV thrombus). Ensure compliance with heart failure medications and dual antiplatelet therapy. Follow-up with cardiologist every 3-6 months for clinical assessment, echo surveillance, and consideration for ICD if LVEF remains ≤35%. In summary, this patient has developed a left ventricular aneurysm 6 weeks post-anterior MI, characterized by apical dyskinesia on echo. Main concerns are heart failure (reduced LV function), ventricular arrhythmias (VT risk 30-50%), and thromboembolism (LV thrombus risk 30-50%, stroke risk 15-20% over 5 years). Management: optimal heart failure therapy, ICD if LVEF <35%, anticoagulation if thrombus develops, and consider surgical aneurysmectomy if refractory symptoms.

question.scenario: A 72-year-old woman presents to her GP 5 days after inferior STEMI treated with primary PCI. She describes sudden onset of severe dyspnoea, orthopnoea, and leg swelling yesterday. On examination, she has bibasal crackles, elevated JVP, peripheral oedema, and a new grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla. Blood pressure is 95/60 mmHg, HR 110 bpm, SpO2 90% on room air. Urgent echocardiography shows severe mitral regurgitation with a flail posterior mitral leaflet.
question.stem: What is the most likely cause, and what is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Acute mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle rupture; urgent surgical mitral valve repair or replacement
options.B: Chronic degenerative mitral regurgitation; medical management with diuretics and vasodilators
options.C: Acute mitral regurgitation from chordae tendineae rupture due to infective endocarditis; prolonged antibiotics
options.D: Functional mitral regurgitation from LV dilatation; medical heart failure therapy and consider MitraClip

mcqs.explanation: Acute mitral regurgitation (MR) from papillary muscle rupture is a rare but catastrophic mechanical complication of acute myocardial infarction, occurring in <1% of MIs in the modern era of early reperfusion (historically 1-2% before primary PCI). It typically occurs 3-7 days post-MI (range 1-14 days) when the infarcted myocardium is weakest, before scar formation. The posteromedial papillary muscle is most vulnerable (blood supply from single artery - PDA), making inferior MI the most common culprit, though anterolateral papillary muscle rupture can occur with anterior MI (dual blood supply from LAD and LCx makes it less common). Papillary muscle rupture causes acute severe mitral regurgitation, leading to sudden haemodynamic collapse with pulmonary oedema, cardiogenic shock, and high mortality (50-90% without surgical intervention). Pathophysiology: The papillary muscles (posteromedial and anterolateral) anchor the mitral valve chordae tendineae to the LV wall, preventing prolapse of mitral leaflets into the left atrium during systole. When a papillary muscle ruptures (complete or partial), the attached chordae lose anchorage, causing flail mitral leaflet. The leaflet prolapses into the LA during systole, allowing massive regurgitant flow from LV to LA. This causes: (1) Volume overload of LA and LV; (2) Acute pulmonary oedema (LA pressure transmitted retrograde to pulmonary veins); (3) Reduced forward cardiac output (blood regurgitates to LA rather than being ejected to aorta); (4) Cardiogenic shock if severe. Complete rupture of an entire papillary muscle head is catastrophic (often fatal within hours). Partial rupture of one head of a papillary muscle (each has 2-3 heads) causes moderate-severe MR with better prognosis if urgently treated. Clinical presentation: (1) Timing: 3-7 days post-MI (median 5 days, as in this case); (2) Sudden onset: Acute deterioration with severe dyspnoea, orthopnoea (pulmonary oedema), hypotension (cardiogenic shock), tachycardia; (3) New murmur: Holosystolic murmur at apex radiating to axilla. Paradoxically, murmur may be SOFT or absent if MR is very severe (equalization of LV and LA pressures reduces pressure gradient and murmur intensity); (4) Pulmonary oedema: Bibasal crackles, tachypnoea, hypoxaemia; (5) Cardiogenic shock: Hypotension, cool peripheries, oliguria, altered mental status (if severe); (6) Echocardiographic findings: Flail mitral leaflet (unattached, mobile), ruptured papillary muscle head visible (may be seen prolapsing into LA or free-floating), severe mitral regurgitation on colour Doppler, dilated LA (though less dilated than chronic MR due to acute onset); (7) Inferior MI: Most cases occur with inferior MI (posteromedial papillary muscle rupture from RCA or LCx occlusion). Differential diagnosis of acute mitral regurgitation post-MI: This patient has sudden severe dyspnoea, pulmonary oedema, new holosystolic murmur, and echo showing severe MR with flail posterior leaflet, occurring 5 days post-inferior MI. Let's differentiate the causes of acute MR: (1) Papillary muscle rupture (Option A): CORRECT DIAGNOSIS. This patient has classic features: (a) Timing: 5 days post-inferior MI (typical for papillary muscle rupture, when infarcted myocardium weakest); (b) Inferior MI: Posteromedial papillary muscle most vulnerable; (c) Sudden onset severe dyspnoea and pulmonary oedema; (d) New holosystolic murmur at apex radiating to axilla (classic for MR); (e) Cardiogenic shock features: Hypotension (95/60 mmHg), tachycardia (110 bpm), hypoxaemia (SpO2 90%); (f) Echo: Severe MR with flail posterior mitral leaflet (indicates ruptured papillary muscle with detached chordae). This is a surgical emergency requiring URGENT mitral valve repair or replacement. Medical management alone has >90% mortality. (2) Chronic degenerative MR (Option B): INCORRECT. Chronic MR (e.g., from mitral valve prolapse, degenerative disease, rheumatic heart disease) develops gradually over months to years. Patients are typically asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic for prolonged periods due to compensatory LV and LA dilatation. Echo in chronic MR shows enlarged LV and LA. This patient's ACUTE presentation (sudden onset 5 days post-MI) and TEMPORAL RELATIONSHIP to MI clearly indicate acute post-MI MR from papillary muscle rupture, NOT chronic degenerative disease. Chronic MR would NOT cause sudden deterioration and would NOT have flail leaflet on echo. (3) Infective endocarditis with chordae rupture (Option C): UNLIKELY. While endocarditis can cause acute MR from chordae tendineae rupture or leaflet perforation, it typically presents with prolonged fever, bacteraemia (positive blood cultures), systemic embolic phenomena (splinter haemorrhages, Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, Roth spots), and vegetations on echo (not mentioned here). Endocarditis is uncommon 5 days post-PCI without prolonged indwelling catheters, prosthetic valves, or IVDU. The TEMPORAL RELATIONSHIP to inferior MI and echo finding of flail leaflet (not vegetation) strongly favour papillary muscle rupture, not endocarditis. If endocarditis suspected, blood cultures and TEE would be indicated, but this is NOT endocarditis. (4) Functional MR from LV dilatation (Option D): INCORRECT. Functional MR occurs when LV dilatation and remodelling (from chronic heart failure or previous MI) cause mitral annular dilatation and leaflet tethering, preventing coaptation. Functional MR develops gradually over weeks to months, NOT acutely. Echo in functional MR shows dilated LV, restricted leaflet motion (tethering), and central jet of MR (not flail leaflet). This patient's ACUTE presentation with flail leaflet indicates structural disruption (papillary muscle rupture), NOT functional MR. MitraClip is a percutaneous repair option for functional MR or inoperable degenerative MR, but NOT appropriate for acute papillary muscle rupture (surgical repair/replacement is required). Management of acute MR from papillary muscle rupture: (1) IMMEDIATE STABILIZATION: (a) Oxygen: High-flow oxygen or non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP) for pulmonary oedema; intubation and mechanical ventilation if respiratory failure; (b) Diuretics: IV furosemide to reduce pulmonary congestion; (c) Vasodilators: IV nitrates (glyceryl trinitrate infusion) to reduce afterload and preload, improving forward flow and reducing MR severity. Sodium nitroprusside is alternative; (d) Inotropes: Dobutamine if low cardiac output/cardiogenic shock (improves contractility). Avoid pure vasopressors (noradrenaline) which increase afterload and worsen MR; (e) Intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP): CRITICAL temporizing measure. IABP reduces afterload (aortic diastolic counterpulsation), decreases MR severity, and improves forward cardiac output. IABP is essential as bridge to surgery. (2) URGENT SURGICAL INTERVENTION (DEFINITIVE TREATMENT): (a) Mitral valve repair: Preferred if feasible (papillary muscle reattachment, chordal replacement, annuloplasty). Lower operative mortality and better long-term outcomes than replacement; (b) Mitral valve replacement: If repair not feasible (extensive rupture, friable tissue). Use bioprosthetic or mechanical valve; (c) Timing: URGENT surgery within hours to 24 hours. Delay increases mortality. Surgery is technically challenging due to friable infarcted tissue, but delay is catastrophic; (d) Concomitant CABG: Often performed simultaneously if significant residual coronary disease. (3) AVOID MEDICAL MANAGEMENT ALONE: Medical therapy (diuretics, vasodilators, inotropes) provides temporary stabilization but does NOT address the structural defect. Without surgery, mortality is 50-90%. Even with optimal medical management and IABP, definitive surgical repair/replacement is essential. (4) Prognosis: Surgical mortality for acute papillary muscle rupture repair is high (20-40%) due to acute presentation, cardiogenic shock, and friable tissue. However, surgery is the only life-saving option. Without surgery, mortality is >90%. Survivors typically have good long-term outcomes if surgery successful and LV function preserved. Comparison with other mechanical complications: Post-MI mechanical complications (VSD, papillary muscle rupture, free wall rupture) share similar timing (3-7 days post-MI) but differ in presentation: (1) Papillary muscle rupture: New MR murmur, pulmonary oedema, flail leaflet on echo; (2) VSD: New VSD murmur (harsh pansystolic at left sternal border), left-to-right shunt, step-up in RV oxygen saturation; (3) Free wall rupture: Cardiac tamponade, sudden collapse, pericardial effusion with tamponade physiology on echo. All require urgent surgical intervention with high mortality. Safety-netting: Once stabilized post-surgery, long-term management includes: (1) Standard post-MI therapy: Dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor for 12 months), beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor, statin; (2) Anticoagulation: If mechanical valve implanted (warfarin indefinitely, target INR 2.5-3.5 depending on valve type and position); (3) Heart failure management: If residual LV dysfunction (LVEF <40%), optimize heart failure therapy (ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, aldosterone antagonists, SGLT2 inhibitors); (4) Endocarditis prophylaxis: For mechanical valves or repaired valves, consider prophylactic antibiotics for high-risk dental/surgical procedures (though guidelines vary); (5) Follow-up: Serial echocardiography to assess valve function, LV function, and detect complications (paravalvular leak, prosthetic valve dysfunction, endocarditis). In summary, this patient has acute severe mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle rupture, a catastrophic mechanical complication of inferior STEMI occurring 5 days post-MI. Clinical features: sudden severe dyspnoea, pulmonary oedema, cardiogenic shock, new holosystolic murmur, and flail mitral leaflet on echo. Management: immediate stabilization (oxygen, diuretics, vasodilators, IABP), followed by URGENT surgical mitral valve repair or replacement within hours to 24 hours. Medical management alone has >90% mortality. Surgical mortality is 20-40%, but surgery is the only life-saving option.
